claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has an as-fabricated hierarchical heterostructure.
High-resolution SEM/DIC imaging can quantify mesoscale heterostructural features such as grain boundaries, spatial distributions, and cluster morphology.
Atom probe tomography can provide quantitative short-range-order metrics.
Combining mesoscale imaging and APT-derived features in a machine-learning model will enable prediction of Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior.
The combined model will predict HfNbTiVAl10 behavior more rapidly and accurately than established simulations.
Adding targeted HfNbTiVAl10 experiments to existing HEA databases will make the training data representative of the alloy's heterostructure across specimens.
Mesoscale microstructural features can be associated with deformation and fracture behavior in refractory multi-principal-element alloys.
Short-range order influences macroscopic elastic, yielding, and fracture behavior.
Alloy-specific training will allow the model to capture the influence of hierarchical heterogeneity on mechanical responses.
The machine-learning framework will reduce predictive lead time relative to full-scale simulations.
Prediction turnaround time will be reduced by approximately 50–60%.
Predictive accuracy will improve by approximately 20–30% relative to conventional simulation methods.
The magnitude of improvement depends on microstructural-data representativeness and machine-learning-model robustness.
Finite-element models, constitutive models, and empirical correlations are established baselines for predicting metallic mechanical properties.
The model may underperform on specimens whose mesoscale or atomic features fall outside the training-data range.
An APT sampling volume that is not representative of the bulk heterostructure may degrade model performance.
APT sampling bias, imaging-resolution variation, and database representativeness are sources of predictive uncertainty.
Room-temperature tensile and fracture tests under controlled strain-rate conditions will be used for model development and evaluation.
Prediction errors exceeding 30% across multiple independent test sets are declared to falsify the hypothesis.
A lack of statistically significant correlation between the multiscale features and measured mechanical performance is declared to falsify the hypothesis.
